title: Stubborn Israel, Refined Israel: Leave Babylon
summary: God addresses Israel as a people who use his name without truth, stubborn from birth, and explains that he announced events in advance so that they could not credit their idols. For his own name's sake he has held back his wrath and refined them in the furnace of affliction, and now he announces new things: his chosen ally will act against Babylon. The chapter laments what obedience would have brought, then commands the exiles to leave Babylon with a shout of joy, recalling the water God gave in the wilderness, and closes with a warning that there is no peace for the wicked.
story: Chapter 48 closes the first half of Isaiah 40 to 55. Chapters 40 to 47 have argued that the LORD alone is God, named Cyrus, and announced the fall of Babylon's gods and of Babylon itself. Now the prophet turns back to Israel and speaks with unusual severity. The exiles are the people God will redeem, but they are not redeemed because they are better than others. They have been stubborn and treacherous, and the rescue happens for the sake of God's name. The chapter ends with the command the whole section has been building toward: go out from Babylon. From chapter 49 onward, Cyrus and Babylon fade from view, and the Servant and the restoration of Zion take center stage.
historical:
The command “Leave Babylon” in verse 20 assumes the setting of the late exile, before or around the Persian capture of the city in 539 BC. The decree of Cyrus in 539/538 BC allowed the exiles to return, and the first group went back under Sheshbazzar and later Zerubbabel (Ezra 1 to 3). Not all went: many Judeans had built lives in Babylonia, as Jeremiah had told them to do (Jeremiah 29:4-7), and a large Jewish community remained there for centuries. The command to leave was therefore a real decision, not a formality, and the chapter's urgency reflects that.

The chosen ally of verse 14 is Cyrus, identified by name in 44:28 and 45:1. The chapter's reference to former things foretold and now fulfilled belongs to the same argument about prophecy that runs through these chapters, and it sits within the authorship question discussed in the notes on chapters 40 and 44.
cultural:
Verses 1 and 2 describe the outward markers of belonging to Israel: bearing the name, descending from Judah, swearing oaths by the LORD's name, and identifying with Jerusalem, the holy city. In the ancient world, to swear by a god's name was to call on that god as witness and guarantor, and it was a basic act of loyalty. The charge is that Israel did all this “not in truth or righteousness.”

The image of refining in verse 10 comes from metalwork. Silver ore was heated in a crucible until the impurities separated and could be skimmed off. Deuteronomy 4:20 calls Egypt an iron furnace from which God brought Israel. Here exile is a furnace too, but God says he refined them “not as silver,” which many interpreters take to mean that he did not apply the full heat that a silversmith would, lest nothing be left. The iron neck and bronze forehead of verse 4 were familiar images of obstinacy, a neck that will not bend and a brow that will not blush.
literary: The chapter is a disputation addressed to Israel, and it gathers up the themes of chapters 40 to 47: former and new things, God as first and last, the idols' silence, the call of Cyrus. Its tone, however, is sharper than any chapter since 40, and it opens with an ironic list of Israel's religious credentials that ends with “but not in truth or righteousness.” The phrase “for My own sake” is repeated in verses 9 and 11 as the hinge of the argument. Verse 16 is a notable shift: after God speaks, a new voice says “the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit,” probably the prophet or the Servant. Verses 20 and 21 are a short hymn of departure recalling the exodus, and verse 22, “There is no peace,” says the LORD, “for the wicked”: a refrain that recurs at 57:21, dividing chapters 40 to 66 into sections.

outline.t: Former things foretold, new things announced, to a stubborn people
Refined in the furnace for the sake of God's name
The first and the last sends his ally against Babylon
Leave Babylon with a shout of joy

doctrines.note: God redeems a people who have been stubborn and treacherous, and he does it “for the sake of My name.” Salvation rests on God's character and purpose, not on the worthiness of those he saves.

Exile is described as a furnace of affliction in which God refines his people. Suffering here is not random or meaningless; it is part of God's purifying work, though the text does not say that every suffering is punishment.

“If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river.” God's commands are presented as the way to flourishing, not an arbitrary burden. Their neglect cost Israel dearly.

Verse 16 mentions the Lord GOD, one who is sent, and the Spirit together. Many Christian interpreters have seen here an early hint of the Trinity, while others read it as the prophet describing his own commission. The text itself does not develop a doctrine, but it prepares for later revelation.

words.note: Tsaraph, to refine by smelting, the work of a metalsmith separating silver from dross. God uses it of what he has done to Israel through exile. The image implies both pain and purpose: the fire is meant to purify, not destroy.

Kur, furnace or smelting pot. The furnace of affliction recalls Egypt as the iron furnace from which God first brought Israel. Exile becomes a second Egypt, and the departure from Babylon a second exodus.

Shem, name. It appears five times in this chapter. Israel is called by God's name and swears by it, yet does not honor it. God acts for the sake of his name, meaning his reputation and revealed character among the nations. The chapter turns on the contrast between Israel's careless use of the name and God's jealous care for it.

Shalom, peace or well-being. Israel's peace would have been like a river if it had listened (verse 18), and there is no peace for the wicked (verse 22). The word frames the chapter's closing: peace is the fruit of listening to God.

christ: Several threads of the chapter reappear in the New Testament. The command to leave Babylon (verse 20) is echoed in Revelation 18:4, where a voice from heaven tells God's people to come out of Babylon so as not to share in her sins. The memory of water from the rock (verse 21), drawn from the exodus (Exodus 17; Numbers 20), is interpreted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:4, where he says that the rock that followed Israel was Christ. The title “I am the first, and I am the last” (verse 12) is again spoken by the risen Jesus in Revelation 1:17. And the voice of verse 16, sent by the Lord GOD with his Spirit, has been read by many Christians as anticipating the Servant of chapter 49 and ultimately Jesus, who was sent by the Father and anointed with the Spirit (Luke 4:18). These are connections the New Testament itself makes or invites, not codes hidden in the text.

hard.q: If God knew Israel would be stubborn and treacherous, why did he choose them, and why tell them the future at all?
hard.a:
The chapter faces the question directly. God says he announced events beforehand precisely because Israel was stubborn, so that they could never say their idol had done it. Prophecy was given not because Israel was reliable, but to leave them no way to credit anyone else. God's choice of Israel is never presented in Scripture as a reward for their goodness (compare Deuteronomy 7:7-8 and 9:4-6); it rests on his love and his promise to their ancestors.

Some readers wonder whether such a view makes God's choice arbitrary or makes Israel's failures irrelevant. The chapter holds both God's commitment and Israel's responsibility. God will not abandon his people, but their disobedience has real consequences: “If only you had paid attention.” The exile happened. The rescue comes not by erasing the past but by God's own faithfulness to his name, which is the chapter's final answer to why he bothers with a stubborn people at all.

questions: Israel used God's name “not in truth or righteousness.” What does it look like to carry God's name in a way that is true?
God says he refined his people in the furnace of affliction. How have hard seasons shaped you, and what did they reveal?
The exiles had to choose to leave Babylon. What comfortable places might God be calling you to leave?
